passage: Daycare note, Tuesday lunch. Deepak pushed his bowl of green dal away and shook his head. Pankaj, beside him, was spooning his up happily, humming. Deepak watched him for a long time. Then he picked up his spoon, took a tiny taste, and took another. His big sister, collecting him later, gasped. "He never eats green dal at home!" What I did next: seated Deepak next to Pankaj again for tomorrow's lunch.

qa.q: What did Deepak push away at first?
qa.a: His bowl of green dal.

qa.q: What was Deepak probably feeling as he watched Pankaj?
qa.a: He was probably wary and unsure of the food, then more trusting once he saw Pankaj enjoy it.

qa.q: Why is seating Deepak next to Pankaj a good plan?
qa.a: Seeing another child eat happily seems to help Deepak feel the food is safe to try.

qa.q: How does Deepak's big sister react?
qa.a: She is surprised and delighted, since he never eats green dal at home.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler trying a food only after watching another child eat it happily.

passage: In the New Year holidays in Kyoto, Hiroshi went shopping with his mother for the new school term. At the stationery shop, he pointed at the blue robot pencil case. "That one." "You liked the green one last week," his mother said. "Everyone in my class has the robot one. Tariq has it. Even the teacher said it's nice." "Do you like it?" Hiroshi hesitated. The robot's eyes were a bit strange. But twenty-six people couldn't all be wrong about it. "Yes," he said. His mother bought it. At home, he put it next to his old green one and looked at them for a while. He wasn't sure which he liked. He only knew which one everyone had.

qa.q: Who in Hiroshi's class has the robot pencil case?
qa.a: Tariq has it, and everyone in his class.

qa.q: Why did Hiroshi hesitate when his mother asked if he liked it?
qa.a: He felt unsure, because he thought the robot's eyes were a bit strange but wanted what everyone else had.

qa.q: What question could help Hiroshi choose next time?
qa.a: He could ask himself which one he would pick if nobody in class had either, to find his own preference.

qa.q: How does Hiroshi's mother see his choice?
qa.a: She seems doubtful, remembering he liked the green one and asking whether he really likes the robot case.

grounding: Shows a child wanting the pencil case everyone in class has, less from liking it than from the sense that so many can't be wrong.

passage: Class teacher's note, Holi week. During the last period on Thursday, I saw from the staff room window a group from 9B on the old boundary wall behind the sports shed. It was a dare that has been going round. Ayesha was among them, arms out, looking frightened, while the others laughed and filmed. Her friend Kiran said afterwards that Ayesha had said, "Everyone's doing it, so it must be fine," even though she was shaking. What I did next: I went straight out, had them all come down, and sat with the group in the classroom. I told them their unease was the sensible part of them. I informed the principal and phoned each parent that same afternoon, and the wall is being fenced.

qa.q: Where was the group from 9B?
qa.a: On the old boundary wall behind the sports shed.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling on the wall?
qa.a: She was frightened and shaking, but doubted her own fear because the group seemed comfortable.

qa.q: What did the teacher do the same day to protect the students?
qa.a: Brought them down, talked with the group, informed the principal, phoned every parent that afternoon, and arranged for the wall to be fenced.

qa.q: How might Kiran have felt watching Ayesha?
qa.a: Kiran likely felt worried for Ayesha, which is why Kiran shared what Ayesha had said.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager going along with a risky dare because the group seems comfortable, doubting her own unease, and an adult's same-day protective response.

passage: "Look at the queue outside that café!" Farida said. It was Christmas Eve on Park Street, lights everywhere. "It must be amazing." "We don't even know what they serve," said Tanuja. "Doesn't matter. Fifty people can't be wrong." "Remember the online course you picked last month? The one with five stars?" "It had ten thousand reviews!" "And you said the videos were terrible." Farida laughed. "Okay, that one was bad." They joined the queue anyway. Forty minutes later, they were eating dry sandwiches. The empty place next door, Tanuja noticed through the window, was serving steaming plates of momos to a happy family. Farida chewed slowly. "Maybe the queue was just a queue."

qa.q: How long did they wait in the queue?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling on seeing the queue?
qa.a: Farida felt excited and sure it must be good, trusting the crowd as proof of quality.

qa.q: What could Farida check next time before trusting a crowd or star rating?
qa.a: Farida could look at the menu or read a few detailed reviews, instead of taking popularity as evidence.

qa.q: How does Tanuja see the crowded café?
qa.a: Tanuja is sceptical, pointing out they don't know the food and reminding Farida of the five-star course.

grounding: Shows a young adult choosing a crowded café and a top-rated course by popularity without checking quality.

subtype: Asking whether the crowd knows or just copies [Response]
passage: That spring, half the kasba was enrolling children in the new coaching centre above the fertiliser shop. Sarika heard it at the ration queue, at the temple, from her neighbour Anirban. "Everyone's joining. Results are guaranteed." She nearly signed her son up on the spot. Then she paused. Did any of these people actually know the teachers? Or was everyone joining because everyone else was? She asked around. Nobody had seen results; the centre had opened only in March. So she walked to the house of Master Ji, a retired maths teacher she trusted, who had nothing to gain. He listened and said, "Ask for a free trial class. Watch who teaches." She did. The teacher read from a book and took no questions. She kept her son home.

qa.q: Where was the new coaching centre?
qa.a: Above the fertiliser shop.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling when she nearly signed her son up?
qa.a: She felt pulled along and a little anxious not to miss out, since everyone around her was joining.

qa.q: What steps did Sarika take before joining the crowd?
qa.a: She asked whether people had real information, found nobody had seen results, and checked with Master Ji, a trusted, independent source.

qa.q: How does Anirban seem to see the coaching centre?
qa.a: Anirban seems convinced it is good simply because everyone is joining.

grounding: Illustrates an adult asking whether a crowd has real information or is copying, and checking with one trusted independent source.

subtype: Playground story grows with each telling [Actor]
passage: The power went out on Diwali night, just as Mummy sent Tushar to fetch the extra diyas from Suraj's house across the park. Across the park meant past the old banyan tree. On Monday, one boy had said the tree was haunted. By Wednesday, three more had said it, adding a white shape and a crying sound. By Friday, the whole class knew for sure. Now, in the dark, with only the flicker of neighbours' diyas, Tushar's heart thumped. The more times he'd heard it, the truer it felt. He ran past, eyes shut, and banged on Suraj's door. "Did you see it?" Suraj whispered. "I didn't look!" Suraj's grandfather laughed. "I've sat under that tree fifty years. Only bats."

qa.q: How long has Suraj's grandfather sat under the banyan tree?
qa.a: Fifty years.

qa.q: Why did Tushar's heart thump as he passed the tree?
qa.a: He felt scared, because hearing the haunted story again and again had made it feel truer each time.

qa.q: What could Tushar ask the next time a scary story spreads through class?
qa.a: Where it started and whether anyone actually saw anything, instead of counting how many people repeat it.

qa.q: How does Suraj's grandfather see the haunted tree story?
qa.a: He finds it funny, knowing from fifty years under the tree that there are only bats.

grounding: Shows a child believing a haunted-tree story more after hearing it retold by many classmates.

passage: I'm Akash, and I watched a rumour eat our school in two weeks. It started in the bus: someone said Gautam Sir, our new physics teacher, had been thrown out of his last school. Nobody knew why. By the next day, there was a reason: he'd shouted at a student. By Friday, the student had been "hurt". People stopped asking him doubts. In the corridor, girls whispered when he passed. I noticed that every person who told me the story said "everyone knows." But nobody knew who had seen anything. I asked my cousin, who'd been at his old school. "He left because his wife got a job here," she said. I told three friends. It barely made a dent. By then, the rumour felt like a fact.

qa.q: Where did the rumour about Gautam Sir start?
qa.a: In the bus.

qa.q: What might Akash have felt after the cousin's answer barely made a dent?
qa.a: Akash probably felt frustrated and uneasy, seeing how hard it is to undo a story everyone already believes.

qa.q: What could students do before repeating a rumour about a teacher?
qa.a: Ask who actually saw anything and check with someone who knows, as Akash did, instead of saying "everyone knows".

qa.q: What is it like for Gautam Sir during those two weeks?
qa.a: He likely feels confused and isolated as students stop asking him doubts and whisper when he passes.

grounding: Illustrates a student observing a rumour about a teacher grow with each repetition until everyone treats it as fact.

passage:
Damini,
The monsoon's been so bad, and yesterday I got that message about the tap water in our area having something dangerous in it. I got it from five different groups: my cousins, my hostel group, even my aunt's colony group. So I forwarded it to everyone I know. Then you replied, "Where is this from? I can't find it on the municipal site." Honestly, it felt a bit cold. Like you don't care if people get sick. Everyone else was sharing it. If it came from so many people, it must be something, right? But I looked again this morning, and I can't find where it started either. The corporation hasn't said anything. I don't know. Maybe you're right to ask. I still feel weird about it.
Jahnavi

qa.q: How many groups did Jahnavi get the message from?
qa.a: Five different groups.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel when Damini asked where the message was from?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt hurt, finding the question cold, as if doubting meant not caring about people getting sick.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi do before forwarding such messages?
qa.a: Check the original source, such as the municipal site, instead of treating how often it appears as proof.

qa.q: How does Damini see the message?
qa.a: Damini is doubtful, unable to find it on the municipal site and wanting to know where it came from.

grounding: Shows a young adult forwarding a scare message because many others have, taking frequency as proof and feeling a doubter is cold.

passage: I'm Kashish, and I've been watching my colony for a month now. It started with one news story from another city: a child snatched from a park. Horrible, and rare. But it was shared everywhere. Within days, parents here stopped letting children play in our park, even in daylight. My neighbour Lakshmi, who used to sit on the bench chatting, now keeps her daughter indoors. There's a new colony group just for "suspicious people". Meanwhile, every morning, the same children are driven through the main road crossing, where cars speed and there's no zebra line. Two scooters collided there last week. Nobody posted about that. I don't blame anyone for being scared. I just see the fear pointing at the wrong thing.

qa.q: Where do the cars speed every morning?
qa.a: At the main road crossing, where there's no zebra line.

qa.q: What does Kashish seem to feel about the colony's reaction?
qa.a: Kashish seems uneasy and a little sad, understanding the fear but troubled that it ignores everyday risks.

qa.q: What could Kashish suggest to the colony group?
qa.a: Kashish could gently point out the dangerous crossing and suggest a zebra line or a volunteer at school time, while keeping the park open with adults nearby.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi's daughter feel kept indoors?
qa.a: Lakshmi's daughter may feel bored and confused about why she can no longer play in the park.

grounding: Illustrates an adult observing a vivid news story about a rare event driving local over-caution while common risks are ignored.

subtype: Checking source and base rate before spreading [Response]
passage: In a rainy London flat, Jamal's phone buzzed: the family group again. His aunt had forwarded a long message: a new scam where criminals spray something on a letter that makes you faint. "FORWARD TO EVERYONE!" Jamal's first instinct was to pass it on. Instead, he searched for the original. It led to a years-old blog with no sources. He checked the police site: no such warning. His flatmate Jin looked over. "Is it real?" "Can't find a single real case." Jamal didn't forward it. He typed to his aunt: "Khala, I checked, and I can't find the police saying this anywhere. It's scary, I know. But I think it's an old rumour. Here's the police page with real scam warnings." She replied with a thumbs up.

qa.q: Where did the original message lead when Jamal searched?
qa.a: To a years-old blog with no sources.

qa.q: What was Jamal's first instinct, and what does it suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: His first instinct was to forward it, suggesting a flash of worry and a wish to protect his family.

qa.q: How did Jamal stop the chain kindly?
qa.a: He checked the source and the police site, didn't forward it, and gently explained to his aunt with a link to real warnings.

qa.q: How might Jamal's aunt feel reading his reply?
qa.a: She might feel reassured and a little relieved, seeing he took her worry seriously.

grounding: Shows an adult tracing a scare claim to its source, checking how common it is, not forwarding it, and gently explaining to a relative.
